description.en:
A topic-wise e-book on the geography of Assam — the Brahmaputra and Barak river valleys, the hills of Karbi Anglong and Dima Hasao, climate and floods, forests and wildlife, agriculture, minerals, and the borders and transport of the state.

This is an online reading e-book only. It cannot be downloaded as a PDF.
description.as:
অসমৰ ভূগোলৰ বিষয়-ভিত্তিক ই-বুক — ব্ৰহ্মপুত্ৰ আৰু বৰাক উপত্যকা, কাৰ্বি আংলং আৰু ডিমা হাছাওৰ পৰ্বত, জলবায়ু আৰু বানপানী, বন আৰু বন্যপ্ৰাণী, কৃষি, খনিজ সম্পদ, আৰু ৰাজ্যখনৰ সীমান্ত আৰু যোগাযোগ।

এই ই-বুক কেৱল অনলাইন পঠনৰ বাবে। ইয়াক PDF হিচাপে ডাউনলোড কৰিব নোৱাৰি।

content.en:
The geography of Assam is dominated by the Brahmaputra valley in the north and the Barak valley in the south. The Brahmaputra enters India near the town of Sadiya in Arunachal Pradesh, passes through Assam from east to west and meets the sea through Bangladesh. The river is joined by important north-bank tributaries like the Subansiri, the Manas and the Sankosh, and south-bank tributaries such as the Dibang, the Dhansiri and the Kopili.

The state is surrounded by highlands. The Karbi Anglong plateau and the Dima Hasao (North Cachar) hills lie in the central part of the state, while the state shares the foothills of the Himalayas with Bhutan and Arunachal Pradesh. The Barak valley in southern Assam is narrow and fertile and is drained by the Barak river and its tributaries.

The two hills are rich in natural beauty and minerals. The Langpi Dehangani and the Barail ranges are notable. Assam also has a number of wetlands, important among them being the Deepor Beel near Guwahati, which is a Ramsar site, while Majuli, the largest river island in the world, is formed in the Brahmaputra near Jorhat.

Assam has a tropical monsoon climate with heavy rainfall. The south-west monsoon brings most of the rain from June to September. The rainfall decreases from the plains to the hills in some regions, but the state as a whole receives abundant rain, and the temperature remains mild for most of the year with high humidity.

Floods are a recurring natural disaster in Assam. The Brahmaputra and its tributaries overflow every year, especially after heavy rain, causing loss of life, property and crops and leading to soil erosion. The annual floods also deposit fertile silt but the government has set up the Brahmaputra Board and various anti-erosion schemes to manage the problem.

Assam is rich in forests and wildlife. The famous national parks are Kaziranga, the home of the one-horned rhinoceros, and Manas, which is both a national park and a tiger reserve. Other protected areas are the Orang, Dibru-Saikhowa and Nameri national parks and the Pobitora wildlife sanctuary, which has the highest density of rhinos in the world. The state has several wildlife sanctuaries and the Hollongapar (Gibbon) sanctuary protects the only ape of India, the hoolock gibbon.

Rice is the principal food crop of Assam, grown in three seasons — Ahu, Sali and Boro. Tea is the most important plantation crop and Assam is one of the largest tea-producing regions of the world. Other crops include jute, sugarcane, mustard, pulses and fruits, and the state is known for its oranges from Tinsukia and pineapples.

Assam is rich in minerals. Oil was first discovered in India at Digboi in 1889, and oil and natural gas are produced from the fields of Digboi, Naharkatia, Moran and Lakwa. Coal is found in the Makum coalfields of Tinsukia district, and limestone is found in the hills of Dima Hasao and Karbi Anglong. The state has a high potential for hydro-electric power.

Assam shares international borders with Bhutan and Bangladesh and national borders with Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram, Meghalaya, Tripura and West Bengal. The Siliguri corridor, popularly called the Chicken's Neck, connects the north-eastern states with the rest of India. Transport in Assam depends on the national highways, the railways, the Brahmaputra waterways and the Lokpriya Gopinath Bordoloi International Airport at Guwahati.
